question: A 7-year-old boy with APSGN has blood pressure 148/96 mmHg, oliguria, periorbital oedema, and serum K+ 5.8 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Steroids are NOT indicated in APSGN; the glomerular injury is immune-complex mediated and self-limiting. Steroids may worsen fluid retention and hypertension.

answers.text: Restrict fluid and salt intake, and give antihypertensive therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. APSGN management is supportive: restrict salt and fluid to match output plus insensible losses, treat hypertension (nifedipine or labetalol acutely), and monitor electrolytes closely.
A 10-day course of penicillin eradicates residual streptococcal carriage but does not alter the course of nephritis; the primary management is supportive, not antibiotic escalation.

answers.text: Perform immediate renal biopsy to guide therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Renal biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations (no latent period, persistent hypocomplementaemia >8 weeks, rapidly progressive course). Classic APSGN is a clinical diagnosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Management of APSGN is supportive: fluid and salt restriction, antihypertensives for elevated BP, and monitoring. Steroids are contraindicated. Penicillin eradicates streptococcal carriage but does not change the nephritis course.
APSGN management is primarily supportive — fluid/salt restriction and antihypertensive therapy. Steroids are not indicated.
